items.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach
items.summary: Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach allowed hackers to access customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets, giving customers until December 8 to migrate their services and download their data. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company announced the shutdown in a new security notification sent to customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, saying it had decided to discontinue the service after reviewing the incident. "Following a review of the situation, Rackspace has made the decision to wind down the Rackspace Spot service. This decision is being made to provide a clear path forward for customers," reads the notification. Rackspace says the service will be permanently discontinued on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when all remaining workloads will be terminated, and customer data will no longer be accessible. Customers have been instructed to retrieve their data and migrate their workloads to different platforms before the deadline. The decision comes after hackers breached Rackspace Spot on November 17 using compromised credentials, allowing them to create unauthorized pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes.

Rackspace says the service will be permanently discontinued on December 8, 2026, at 5 PM Central Time, when all remaining workloads will be terminated, and customer data will no longer be accessible.

Customers have been instructed to retrieve their data and migrate their workloads to different platforms before the deadline.

The decision comes after hackers breached Rackspace Spot on November 17 using compromised credentials, allowing them to create unauthorized pods in customer Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes.

items.title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
items.summary: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: - The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; - Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed.

items.title: Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations
items.summary: Threat actors have exploited multiple vulnerabilities to compromise two dozen Check Point Security management servers in an ongoing campaign targeting 22 organizations. Threat intelligence firm GreyNoise detected the activity, noting that it resembled cyberespionage operations, although the attacker's motivation could not be conclusively determined. The researchers track the activity as GT13 and confirmed it was ongoing between October 17 and November 2, when their visibility ended. However, given the threat actor's persistent access to Check Point devices, they believe the campaign remains active. GreyNoise says the 22 victim organizations are spread across 17 countries, and show no clear evidence of specific targeting. They include government entities, financial services providers, and companies in the energy, transportation, mining, and manufacturing sectors. The attacks were launched from 99 IP addresses that appear to come from compromised Check Point devices and ExpressVPN exit nodes. A Rejetto HTTP File Server, compromised by exploiting CVE-2026-61500, was used as an operational relay for managing intrusions and collecting stolen data from the compromised environments. While GreyNoise could not determine when or how the Check Point servers were breached, it observed the exploitation of CVE-2026-16232 during the post-compromise stages.

items.title: Volant Manticore: Flying Under the Radar
items.summary: Key Points - Check Point Research identified Volant Manticore, a previously undocumented Iranian threat group linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). Based on our observations, we believe this is the first Iranian group to designate Cyprus as a primary espionage target, focusing on telecommunications companies, airlines, and critical infrastructure. - The group uses KuboShell, a new backdoor that utilizes IPFS for command-and-control (C2) functions, to deploy the Homa Framework, a post-compromise framework built on a reimplementation of MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go client. Alongside custom malware, Volant Manticore delivers RMM tools and runs credential-harvesting campaigns. - Further analysis shed light on the operators’ internal setup, including development, testing, and operational environments, both on-premise and in the cloud. We observed the group testing their tooling against antivirus products before deployment, as well as using Fortinet SSL VPN clients which suggests access to the victims’ networks via VPN. - While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster. - Volant Manticore’s targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments. A recent shift toward Saudi Arabian targets, including the healthcare sector, may reflect the escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

- The group uses KuboShell, a new backdoor that utilizes IPFS for command-and-control (C2) functions, to deploy the Homa Framework, a post-compromise framework built on a reimplementation of MuddyWater’s MuddyC2Go client. Alongside custom malware, Volant Manticore delivers RMM tools and runs credential-harvesting campaigns.
- Further analysis shed light on the operators’ internal setup, including development, testing, and operational environments, both on-premise and in the cloud. We observed the group testing their tooling against antivirus products before deployment, as well as using Fortinet SSL VPN clients which suggests access to the victims’ networks via VPN.
- While we identified multiple links to MuddyWater, we assess that Volant Manticore likely consists of former MuddyWater operators who branched off from the group and currently operate as a separate threat cluster.
- Volant Manticore’s targeting priorities appear responsive to regional geopolitical developments. A recent shift toward Saudi Arabian targets, including the healthcare sector, may reflect the escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis.

items.title: Cyberattacks involving AI agents: First confirmed cases in Switzerland
items.summary: In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent. Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks. In all cyberattacks known to the NCSC, the use of AI agents led to the successful compromise of the victim’s IT systems. These cases represent a shift in the cyber threat landscape. The NCSC anticipates an increase in the number of rapid and successful cyberattacks. It therefore strongly advises companies and operators of critical infrastructure to take necessary measures to enhance their cyber security and resilience.

items.title: South Korea’s power giant KEPCO confirms data breach impacting 1.5 million
items.summary: A threat actor breached the internal network of Korea Electric Power Corporation (KEPCO) and accessed two systems containing customer, employee, and contractor data. The attack exposed details of more than 1.5 million individuals before the company blocked access from external IP addresses and suspended the affected services. KEPCO is South Korea’s main electric power company and a state-controlled, major operator of the country’s critical infrastructure. The organization detected the attack on November 20, when it confirmed unauthorized access to its KEPCO ON electricity billing platform and its electronic procurement system (SRM). “On Friday, November 20, Korea Electric Power Corporation (hereafter KEPCO), led by President Kim Dong-cheol, confirmed that some customer information held in its IT systems had been exposed,” the power company states. “The company is making every effort to prevent harm.” ON is an integrated customer platform that allows customers to view and pay electricity bills. SRM is the company’s procurement system for contracting services. According to the announcement, published on Sunday, the following was exposed: - for 650,487 KEPCO ON customers: names, ID information, phone numbers, addresses, bank names, bank account numbers, account holder names, card issuers, card numbers, cardholder names, and electricity charge and billing information. - for 426,827 company representatives: names, ID information, email addresses, and company addresses. - for 442,934 KEPCO employees: names, affiliation, employee ID number, mobile phone number, email address, company phone number.

items.title: European Commission confirms personal data stolen in AI-assisted cyberattack
items.summary: The European Commission has confirmed that hackers made off with personal data in the AI-assisted cyberattack disclosed last week, but has relied on a website notice rather than contacting affected users directly. Speaking at a press briefing on Monday, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed that EU Academy, an online learning platform offering courses on EU policies and initiatives, was among the systems compromised during the cyber campaign targeting the bloc's executive arm. The stolen data includes the names and email addresses of people outside the EU institutions, though the Commission has yet to figure out how many users are affected or whether other personal information was compromised. Public access to the platform has been disabled as a precaution. Despite confirming the theft, the Commission hasn't contacted affected individuals directly. Instead, it has posted a notice on the EU Academy website, a decision Regnier defended when quizzed by reporters on Monday. "There was no reach out to individual users, but rather a general message to all users on the website out of transparency," Regnier said. The notice warns users that they could find themselves on the receiving end of spearphishing attacks, impersonation attempts, and spam as a result of the breach. The Commission is also advising users not to hand over personal information to anyone who contacts them claiming to be involved in EU Academy activities.

items.title: Familiar weaknesses, exploited faster: defending against agentic cyber attacks
items.summary: Since September 2026, the NCSC has seen a marked rise in AI-assisted cyber attacks. Organisations across multiple sectors are reporting incidents as a result of threat actors using ‘agentic offensive frameworks'; software originally designed for red teaming being applied beyond its defensive purpose. The incidents involved automated identification and exploitation attempts across organisations' internet-facing services and assets in quick succession. This resulted in downtime to some services or the compromise of systems, providing attackers with a foothold for further agent-driven activity (or in some cases, human-driven activity within their network). It’s worth noting that: - none of the weaknesses being exploited are new or novel - the tools the agents have access to are common and provide no new capability the typical threat actor would have access to What has changed, is how quickly and persistently threat actors can conduct attacks – at low cost – using these frameworks combined with cheap, capable open models or illegal API resellers. This blog explains how agentic offensive frameworks are being used, what this means for cyber defenders, and the steps you should take to help protect your organisation.
